body: You can usually calculate filteredItems from the list and query during render.
Start at the address bar and tab through the page. You should always see where focus is.
Check that dialogs return focus to the button that opened them.
Try Shift+Tab as well. Our menu only worked in one direction.
For a single author foreign key, yes, select_related is the first thing I'd try.
Use prefetch_related for the team members if that's a many-to-many relationship.
Measure it again after the change. It is easy to fix authors and still fetch each avatar separately.
Got it down from 42 to 4 queries. The tags were the other part.
I'd expect the normal browse view when I clear the input.
Depends whether it's a dedicated search dialog or the main list page.
We show all items but keep any category filters. Clearing text shouldn't reset those.
Good point about keeping filters. I'll test that version.
For a day-only deadline use a date column and avoid converting midnight UTC into local time.
We had this bug when calling new Date on a date-only string and formatting it locally.
Put a short working/not-yet-working list near the top.
A setup command and one screenshot help more than a huge feature wishlist.
Include the known rough edges. It makes it easier for someone to give useful feedback.
If the browser talks directly to the database, database policies need to enforce it too.
I'd pick the one you can test with a real person this week.
Show the sample size and how you recruited people.
I'd show counts alongside percentages. With 23 responses the percentages look more precise than they are.
Mention who didn't respond too, if you know. Our survey only reached students already in the club.
Try preserving the visible item's position instead of scrolling to an absolute offset.
Stable keys on list items helped in our prototype.
Are you recreating the scroll controller on every build?
It was the controller. Moving it into the state object fixed most of the jump.
Expected result, actual result, and the shortest steps to reproduce.
Add browser/device if it's a UI problem.
A short screen recording helps, but don't make a video mandatory.
Please include the input that triggered it. 'Search is broken' took us an hour to reproduce.
If saving personal data isn't the point, a local prototype might be enough.
We used example inputs and no accounts for the first user test.
Make a branch or commit your current work before resolving it.
Read both changes with your teammate. The correct result might include parts of both.
Don't just choose 'accept incoming' for every conflict. Run the app afterwards.
That comparison is a result. Explain the dataset and where the model fails.
The smallest snippet that still reproduces the problem, plus the exact error.
Don't silently change the count to zero. That hides a reconciliation problem.
I'd record the correction and show a warning, but ask the shop how they handle it now.
We separated the transaction ledger from the displayed stock estimate.
Colour can help, but the labels need to remain usable where lines cross.
Try printing it in grayscale and zooming to 200 percent.
A data table is useful for readers who can't use the chart at all.
Dash styles helped our two similar blue lines. We kept the direct labels too.
Try drawing the two tables before writing the query.
I'm working on the same thing. A small book-and-author dataset made it click for me.
Start with an inner join, then ask which unmatched rows a left join keeps.
Don't rush into five-table examples. Two tables can teach a lot.
Send a private check-in first. There may be something going on.
Make the remaining work visible so the rest of the team can plan without guessing.
Use a clearly labelled demo dataset with relationships that actually make sense.
Show an empty state too. Handling a new account is part of the product.
A small believable example tells me more than a screenshot with 50,000 users.
Rotate the key. Deleting it from the latest file doesn't remove it from history.
Test the rounding and split calculation. Those are easy to get subtly wrong.
Ask what they expected to happen at the point they paused.
Watch the task first, then ask about specific moments rather than a general rating.
Avoid explaining the interface while they're trying it. I kept doing that by accident.
Use a CSV parser that handles quoted fields. A different separator won't solve every case.
Test quotes inside quoted text too.
Keep an import report with row numbers so someone can fix a bad record.
We were splitting on commas by hand. Replaced that with the standard csv module.
Write one observable outcome and how to check it.
'Save a draft and restore it after reload' is easier to finish than 'do frontend'.
Add dependencies if another task genuinely blocks it.
We now include a small done checklist. Two or three items is usually enough.
A generic placeholder mark avoids implying endorsement.
Check the institution's published brand rules if you want to use its actual logo.
Use a month name where the space allows it.
For date-only deadlines, be careful not to apply a timezone conversion.
A full date in the tooltip is useful but shouldn't be the only readable label.
Start by checking which columns are latitude and longitude.
Nice catch. Put the rule in the database transaction, not just a disabled button.
Read recent discussions to see whether someone is already working on it.
Try running the project locally before promising a fix.
A short question about the expected behaviour can save a lot of work.
Fix anything that prevents completing the main task with a keyboard.
Check labels and error messages on the main form.
Keep the remaining issues visible instead of calling the whole app accessible.
We split blockers from improvements and added a person responsible for each.
A documented setup and pinned dependencies may solve enough for now.
Docker can help with the database, but adds another thing to learn.
We containerised only PostgreSQL first and kept the app outside it.
Whatever you choose, try the instructions on a clean machine.
Keep missing distinct from an actual zero.
Report how many responses each question has.
Have a local screenshot or recording of the main flow as a fallback.
Demo one complete task instead of every menu item.
Make the example data ahead of time so you aren't typing long forms on stage.
First decide whether persistence is needed and explain it to users.
Testing the problem with potential users is real project work.
Agree on a specific demonstration and the limitations you'll explain.
A reproducible experiment can be more valuable than a polished extra screen.
Write a small acceptance checklist with your supervisor.
Look at texture sizes before chasing tiny mesh savings.
Measure the exported file, not just the Blender project size.
Could a still image explain the project just as well on mobile?
We kept an optional 3D view and loaded a small poster image first.
Pick one trade-off you're unsure about and explain your current choice.
Tell them what the app is meant to do and how to run it.
A small pull request is easier to review than an entire repo.
I asked about my permission checks and got much more useful feedback than on naming every file.
Transfer a fictional balance between two accounts and make the second update fail.
Try reserving the last seat with two requests at once.
Label it 'tasks completed' rather than suggesting it measures all effort.
We show done/total next to the bar so the meaning is clear.
Don't invent precision. A milestone summary can be more honest for some projects.
Check the image orientation metadata and whether your processing library applies it.
Return a stable public message and keep detailed diagnostics server-side.
Try the manual workflow first and see what actually repeats.
Consent and unsubscribe handling matter even for a small list.
Use an existing mailing tool before writing your own sender.
Pick a task and explain where you weren't sure what to click.
Separate the issue from your preferred solution.
Try 'I missed the save button after editing' instead of 'make it pop'.
Asking what they want feedback on helps too. They might still be working on the layout.
You're counting combinations from both joins. Aggregate separately or count the distinct thing you mean.
Draw one project with two members and three tasks; the joined result has six rows.
Be careful with COUNT DISTINCT as a blanket fix. Check the other aggregates too.
The six-row example made it click. I moved each count into its own subquery.
Ask someone to follow your instructions without coaching them.
Write down prerequisites and what successful output looks like.
Keep both versions when the text differs and let the user choose.
Separate fields that can merge safely from fields that need a decision.
Start by making the conflict visible. Automatic merging can come later.
Yes, if you explain what you learned and what evidence changed your mind.
Nice! Try documenting the Python version as well.
At least include the discussion title so the user knows where they landed.
If you can, link to the specific reply and highlight it briefly.
Think about what the link does if the comment was removed.
List what you can discuss and mark your current level honestly.
A project showing how you used a tool helps more than a huge skills list.
Keep 'learning' separate from things you can help someone with.
I removed a few tools and linked the projects where I actually used the rest.
No. Leave a clear status and a note about what remains.
Archive it if nobody expects to return soon, but keep the write-up.
A working small piece can still help the next team.
We recorded a two-minute walkthrough before pausing. Glad we did.
A setup guide that someone outside the team has actually followed.
Include a small sample dataset, with no real account details in it.
We recorded the main flow and the known failures in a short screen recording.
Who owns the deployment account? Sort that out before everyone leaves.
Thanks, that is the bit we had missed. It is still under my personal account.
Move ownership through the service settings. Do not put a shared password in the README.
Leave a list of decisions too, especially the things you deliberately did not build.
We have booked a handover session where the new team does the setup and we only take notes.
We tried a five-line brief. Problem, who it helps, one flow, what is out of scope, and how we will test it.
The out-of-scope line saved us. Otherwise someone adds a payment system in week two.
Do you write it before talking to users or after?
A rough version before, then change it after the first conversation. It is a hypothesis at that point.
I would keep the success measure separate from the feature list. Finishing the features does not prove they help.
Ours said "students can find an available room". We changed it to finding one in under a minute using the list view.
How many people did you test with?
Only four for the first pass, so we treated it as usability feedback, not evidence about the whole campus.
We also wrote down the devices they used. Two problems only happened on phones.
Agree on testing early, but a stopwatch can make people rush. Ask them to think aloud in a separate pass.
Good point. We will do the first pass without timing it.
Our brief includes who can make a scope decision when teammates disagree. That avoided a few stalled meetings.
We use one person for each decision, but anyone can leave a concern in the notes.
A sketch helped us more than another paragraph. It made the different assumptions visible.
I have cut our brief from three pages to half a page and added the sketch. Much easier to discuss now.
Leave a dated copy when the scope changes. It makes the final reflection easier to write.
